Moth
MAWTH
noun
From the Saxon moththe, a small nocturnal insect whose larva feeds upon wool and cloth; rendering the Hebrew 'ash, the fretting insect of the garment, and the Greek ses, used by our Lord in the Sermon on the Mount.

Biblical Definition

The moth is the small insect whose larva eats wool, and in Scripture it is the standing emblem of decay working quietly from within. Its work is not violent; nobody hears a moth. The garment is folded away, apparently safe, and comes out ruined. So Job says of frail man that he “consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten” (Job 13:28), and Isaiah says of the accusers of the Servant that “they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up” (Isa 50:9) — the whole apparatus of opposition quietly consumed while the Servant stands justified. Hosea says something more solemn still: “I will be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness” (Hos 5:12). God Himself can be the slow decay in a nation’s cloth, a judgment that does not thunder but eats. Our Lord takes the same image and makes it the argument of the Christian’s whole treasury: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:19), but lay up treasure in heaven, “where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). The reasoning is not that earthly goods are wicked but that they are perishable, and a wise man does not build where the builders are moth and rust. Where the treasure is, there the heart follows; the moth is God’s standing witness that the heart must go somewhere higher.

Webster 1828 Definition

A small insect whose larva devours cloth; the biblical emblem of quiet, unstoppable decay against which heavenly treasure is laid up.

expand to see more

MOTH, a small nocturnal insect whose larva eats and destroys wool and cloth.

From the Saxon moththe; kindred with the Dutch mot.

Renders the Hebrew 'ash and the Greek ses.

Figuratively, anything that secretly and gradually consumes.

Used by our Lord for the perishableness of all earthly treasure (Mat 6:19).

Key Scripture

Mat 6:19 — "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:"

Mat 6:20 — "But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:"

Job 13:28 — "And he, as a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten."

Isa 50:9 — "Behold, the Lord GOD will help me; who is he that shall condemn me? lo, they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up."

Modern Corruption

The moth is answered with better storage — insurance, diversification, permanence purchased — when our Lord named it to move the treasure, not to protect it.

expand to see more

The commonest evasion of Mat 6:19 is to hear it as a problem of security rather than of location. Moth and rust corrupt, therefore build a better vault: preserve, insure, hedge, endow, and the decay is defeated. Every age has its version of the strategy and every age discovers the same thing, that the moth is patient and the vault is not eternal. Our Lord did not say earthly treasure was insufficiently guarded. He said it was in the wrong place. The whole force of the command falls on the word where. There is a country in which nothing eats, and He is telling His disciples to bank there.

The remedy is not asceticism, which is only another way of making earthly goods the centre of attention. Scripture commends provision for one’s house, honest labour, the inheritance a good man leaves to his children’s children. But it treats every one of those as a stewardship passing through the hand, not a treasure resting in the heart — for the heart follows the treasure, and a heart lodged among moth-eaten things will be moth-eaten too. Laying up treasure in heaven is done here, in mercy shewn, in the poor relieved, in the gospel sent, in a life spent for Christ. What is given away is the only part of an estate the moth cannot reach.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The cloth-eating insect — quiet decay in a garment, and the measure of everything laid up on earth.

expand to see more

Moth — Saxon moththe, the insect whose larva devours wool.

Hebrew 'ash; Greek ses in the words of our Lord.

Job 13:28 makes it the figure of man’s frailty, consumed like a moth-eaten garment.

Isa 50:9 turns it on the Servant’s accusers — they wax old and the moth eats them up.

Hos 5:12: the LORD Himself as a moth to Ephraim — judgment that eats rather than thunders.

Usage

"Nobody hears a moth — which is exactly why it is the emblem of decay."

"The command of Mat 6:19 is about where, not about how well the vault is built."

"What is given away is the only part of an estate the moth cannot reach."
